title: Scaling Vision Transformers for Functional MRI with Flat Maps
claim: Data representations lie on a spectrum from too dense to too lossy, and an intermediate representation is best.
layout: 3 stacked rows, left-to-right patching, vertical gradient arrow on left
description: Three horizontal rows show the same brain activity in three representations: volume, flat map and parcellation. Each row has a gray rounded box with the data on the left. An arrow passes through a box labeled "patch" and points to a 2x4 grid of example patches on the right. The volume row has 3D brain renderings and cube patches. The flat map row has two flattened cortical sheets and square 2D patches. The parcellation row has a grid of colored dots and single-dot patches. A vertical red-to-white-to-blue gradient arrow on the left reads "too dense" at the top, "goldilocks zone" in the middle (boxed, around the flat map row) and "too lossy" at the bottom. Warm yellow/orange and cool blue colors show activation values. The eye goes first to the colorful brains and the gradient bar.
caption: Spectrum of fMRI data representations: volume is the native 3D MRI format, flat map is our proposed representation based on cortical flat map projection, and parcellation data results from averaging signal within a set of regions (parcels). Volume patches are 3D cubes, flat map patches are 2D squares, and parcellation "patches" are single scalars. We hypothesize there is a "goldilocks zone" of representations that are neither too lossy nor too dense.
abstract: We study the problem of training self-supervised foundation models for functional MRI. Our main contributions are: (1) we introduce a new model family (CortexMAE) trained using the masked autoencoder framework on 2.1K hours of open fMRI data, and (2) we release the first open evaluation suite (Brainmarks) for fMRI foundation models. Our core innovation is simple: we adapt the Vision Transformer to fMRI by first converting each 3D fMRI volume to a 2D map using a cortical flat map projection. We directly compare flat maps to both parcellation and volume-based representations. While each has its advantages, flat maps generally perform best. We perform the first systematic scaling analysis for fMRI and observe strict power law scaling, albeit with limits. Finally, we use Brainmarks to do controlled benchmark comparisons. On subject-level trait prediction, we report a challenging null result: no single model achieves clear state-of-the-art performance. Moreover, all models struggle to outperform a simple functional connectivity baseline. On cognitive state decoding, we observe more robust performance, and in this setting our CortexMAE family outperforms prior models by a large margin. Code, models, and datasets are available at https://github.com/MedARC-AI/CortexMAE and https://github.com/MedARC-AI/Brainmarks.
